questions.domain: Design and implement a source control strategy
questions.explanation:
Git rebase moves or replays the commits from one branch onto another, creating brand-new commits with new hashes for each original commit. This process rewrites the commit history, producing a linear sequence rather than preserving the original branching structure, which is what "overriding the history" refers to. Merge, by contrast, preserves the original history of both branches and adds a merge commit rather than rewriting it. Fetch only retrieves updates from a remote without integrating them, and Push only uploads local commits to a remote repository — neither operation integrates changes from another branch while rewriting history the way rebase does.

**Learn more:** [Merging vs. Rebasing | Atlassian Git Tutorial](https://www.atlassian.com/git/tutorials/merging-vs-rebasing) · [Git rebase | Atlassian Git Tutorial](https://www.atlassian.com/git/tutorials/rewriting-history/git-rebase)

questions.domain: Design and implement build and release pipelines
questions.question:
You use Azure Pipelines to build and test code projects.  
  
You notice an increase in cycle times.  
  
You need to identify whether agent pool exhaustion is causing the issue.  
  
What are two possible ways to achieve this goal? Each correct answer presents a complete solution.  
  
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

options.text: View the pool consumption report at the organization level.

questions.explanation: Querying the TaskAgentPoolSizeSnapshots endpoint provides historical agent pool usage snapshots, revealing capacity exhaustion patterns over time. Viewing the pool consumption report at the organization level offers a summary of how agent pools are utilized across projects. Together, these two approaches directly diagnose pool exhaustion as a cycle-time cause.

questions.domain: Implement an instrumentation strategy
questions.question:
You use Azure Pipelines to build and test code projects.  
  
You notice an increase in cycle times.  
  
You need to identify whether agent pool exhaustion is causing the issue.  
  
What are two possible ways to achieve this goal? Each correct answer presents a complete solution.  
  
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

options.text: the Smart Detection feature in Azure Application Insights
the Failures feature in Azure Application Insights
an Azure Monitor alert that uses an Azure Log Analytics query

questions.explanation:
Application Insights Smart Detection (Failure Anomalies) automatically monitors the rate of failed requests using machine learning and proactively alerts when there is an abnormal rise, without requiring you to author or maintain custom queries, thresholds, or alert rules. This built-in, automatic behavior satisfies the requirement to minimize administrative effort, whereas the Failures feature only provides manual investigation views, Azure Service Health covers Azure platform/service outages rather than app-level failures, and a custom Log Analytics-based alert would require ongoing manual query and threshold maintenance.

**Learn more:** [Smart detection in Application Insights - Failure Anomalies](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-monitor/app/proactive-failure-diagnostics) · [Application Insights Smart Detection overview](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-monitor/alerts/proactive-diagnostics)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You manage a project by using Azure Boards. You manage the project code by using GitHub.  
  
You have three work items that have IDs of 456, 457, and 458.  
  
You need to create a pull request that will be linked to all the work items. The solution must set the state of work item 456 to done.  
  
What should you add to the commit message?
questions.explanation: Referencing Azure Boards work items from a GitHub commit requires the "AB#" prefix on each ID; adding an explicit completion marker naming work item 456 specifically transitions only that item to Done while the plain AB# references still link all three work items to the pull request. Among the given choices, using the AB# format for all three IDs plus a separate completion statement for 456 is the closest match to this required syntax and behavior.

questions.domain: Design and implement build and release pipelines
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an app that is deployed to two environments named Production-A and Production-B by using Azure Pipelines.  
  
You need to configure a release pipeline that will mark the app as complete and ready for release into the Production-B environment. The solution must meet the following requirements:  
  
• Ensure that there are no active Azure Monitor alerts in the Production-A environment before the app is marked as complete.  

• Minimize administrative effort.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: To the Production-B environment stage, add a pre-deployment gate that will query Azure Monitor.
To the Production-A environment stage, add a post-deployment gate that will query Azure Monitor.
To the Production-A environment stage, add a post-deployment approval.
To the Production-A environment stage, add a pre-deployment gate that will query Azure Monitor.

questions.explanation: A post-deployment gate on the Production-A stage runs automatically after deployment completes and queries Azure Monitor for active alerts before Azure Pipelines marks that stage as successfully completed, which is the trigger for the pipeline to proceed toward Production-B. A pre-deployment gate on Production-B would check alerts before deploying to B rather than before Production-A is marked complete, and a manual approval doesn't automatically query Azure Monitor.

You have a web application hosted on Azure App Service that stores its data in an Azure SQL database.  
  
You need to generate an alert whenever there are 10,000 simultaneous connections to the database. The solution must minimize development effort.  
  
Which option should you select in the Diagnostics settings of the database?
questions.explanation:
Sending diagnostic data to Log Analytics lets you use Azure Monitor's built-in log search alert rules to evaluate collected metrics (such as connection counts) and trigger notifications automatically, requiring no custom code. Streaming to an Event Hub would require building and maintaining a separate consumer application to process the stream and raise alerts, increasing development effort. Archiving to a storage account only retains diagnostic data for later analysis and does not support real-time alerting. Therefore, routing the diagnostic logs to Log Analytics is the lowest-effort way to configure an alert for a threshold like 10,000 simultaneous connections.

**Learn more:** [Tutorial: Alert on Log Analytics data - Azure Monitor](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-monitor/alerts/tutorial-log-alert) · [Overview of Azure platform logs and diagnostic settings](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-monitor/essentials/diagnostic-settings)

Your company has a release pipeline defined in an Azure DevOps project. You plan to deploy to an Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) cluster by using the Helm package and deploy task.  
  
You need to install a service in the AKS namespace to support the planned deployment.  
  
Which service should you install?
questions.explanation:
Helm v2 uses a client-server model where the Helm CLI communicates with a server-side component called Tiller that runs inside the Kubernetes cluster. Before Helm can package, install, or upgrade charts through the Azure DevOps Helm deploy task, Tiller must be installed into the target namespace (typically via 'helm init'), as it is responsible for executing the actual release operations against the Kubernetes API. Azure Container Registry is merely an external registry for storing images/charts, Chart is just the packaging artifact, and Kubectl is a command-line client rather than an in-cluster service, so none of those fulfill the requirement of an installable service within the AKS namespace.

**Learn more:** [Helm install (Helm 2 Tiller architecture)](https://v2.helm.sh/docs/install/)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an Azure DevOps organization named Contoso that contains a project named Project1. You also have an Azure subscription named Sub1 that includes an Azure key vault named vault1.  
  
You need to ensure that you can reference the values of the secrets stored in vault1 from all the pipelines in Project1. The solution must prevent the secret values from being stored in the pipelines.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Create a variable group in Project1.
Add a secure file to Project1.
Modify the security settings of the pipelines.
Configure the security policy of Contoso.

questions.explanation:
Azure Pipelines lets you create a variable group in the project's Library and link it to an existing Azure key vault. When you link the variable group to Key Vault, only the secret names are stored in the variable group definition; the actual secret values are retrieved directly from Key Vault at pipeline run time via an authorized service connection with Get and List permissions. A variable group can be made available to all pipelines in the project, satisfying the requirement to reference vault1's secrets from every pipeline in Project1 while ensuring the secret values themselves are never persisted in the pipeline definitions.

**Learn more:** [Link a variable group to secrets in Azure Key Vault - Azure Pipelines | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/library/link-variable-groups-to-key-vaults?view=azure-devops) · [Manage variable groups - Azure Pipelines | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/library/variable-groups?view=azure-devops)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your organization runs an application that includes several Azure App Service web apps and Azure Functions. You want to review recommendations concerning the security of these web apps and functions, and you plan to go to the Compute and Apps section to do so.  
  
Which of the following should you access in order to use Compute and Apps?
questions.explanation:
Azure Security Center (rebranded as Microsoft Defender for Cloud) organizes its security recommendations by resource category, and the 'Compute and Apps' section specifically includes recommendations for Azure App Service web apps and Azure Functions, such as enabling managed identities, restricting FTP access, enforcing HTTPS, and using the latest runtime versions. This is distinct from Azure Log Analytics (a log query/data platform), Azure Event Hubs (a data streaming ingestion service), and Azure Advisor (a general best-practices advisor that lacks the specific 'Compute and Apps' navigation grouping used for security posture recommendations).

**Learn more:** [Microsoft Defender for App Service - Benefits and Features](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/defender-for-cloud/defender-for-app-service-introduction) · [Reference table for Azure App Service security recommendations - Microsoft Defender for Cloud](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/defender-for-cloud/recommendations-reference-app-services)

When a new version of Project is released, the latest version is deployed to environment2, and the previous version is redeployed to environment1.  
  
You need to distribute users across the environments. The solution must meet the following requirements:  
  
• New releases must be available to only a subset of the users.  

• You must gradually increase the number of users that can access environment2.  
  
What should you use?
questions.explanation: Web app deployment slots enable gradual rollout of new versions to a percentage of users through traffic distribution. lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You manage an Azure web app that supports an e-commerce website.  
  
You need to increase the logging level when the web app exceeds normal usage patterns. The solution must minimize administrative overhead.  
  
Which two resources should you include in the solution? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.  
  
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

options.text: an Azure Monitor alert that has a dynamic threshold
an Azure Monitor alert that has a static threshold
an Azure Monitor alert that uses an action group that has an email action

questions.explanation:
Detecting when usage deviates from 'normal patterns' requires a dynamic threshold alert, which uses machine learning to establish a baseline from historical data and trigger only on anomalous deviations, rather than a fixed static threshold. To minimize administrative overhead, the response to that alert—raising the logging level—must happen automatically rather than relying on a person to read an email and make the change manually. An Azure Automation runbook can be configured as the alert's action to automatically execute the required change (e.g., updating diagnostic/logging settings) whenever the dynamic threshold alert fires.

**Learn more:** [Dynamic thresholds in metric alerts - Azure Monitor](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-monitor/alerts/alerts-dynamic-thresholds) · [Action groups - Azure Monitor](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-monitor/alerts/action-groups)

questions.question:
Solution: In **Pre-deployment conditions**, modify the **Time between re-evaluation of gates** option.  
  
Does this satisfy the goal?
questions.explanation:
Time between re-evaluation of gates controls how often gates are sampled; it does not control the timeout for a manual approval. An unapproved deployment is rejected when the approval Timeout period expires, so the approval timeout must be set to eight hours to meet the requirement.\
\
**Learn more:** [Control deployments with release approvals - Azure Pipelines](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/release/approvals/approvals?view=azure-devops) · [Deployment gates concepts - Azure Pipelines](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/release/approvals/gates?view=azure-devops)

questions.domain: Design and implement build and release pipelines
questions.question:
Solution: In **Post-deployment conditions**, modify the **Time between re-evaluation of gates** option.  
  
Does this achieve the goal?
questions.explanation:
The gate re-evaluation interval only determines how often automated deployment gates are sampled. A pending manual approval is rejected when its configured approval timeout expires, so the approval timeout—not the post-deployment gate sampling interval—must be set to eight hours.\
\
**Learn more:** [Deployment gates concepts - Azure Pipelines](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/release/approvals/gates?view=azure-devops) · [Control deployments with release approvals - Azure Pipelines](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/release/approvals/approvals?view=azure-devops)

questions.domain: Design and implement build and release pipelines
questions.question:
Solution: In **Pre-deployment conditions**, modify the **Timeout** setting for pre-deployment approvals.  
  
Does this achieve the goal?
questions.explanation:
The pre-deployment approval Timeout determines the period Azure DevOps waits for approval; if no approval is granted within that period, the deployment is rejected. Configuring it for eight hours ensures an unapproved deployment does not fail after two hours and is rejected only after the required eight-hour approval period.\
\
**Learn more:** [Control deployments with release approvals - Azure Pipelines](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/release/approvals/approvals?view=azure-devops)

questions.domain: Implement an instrumentation strategy
questions.question:
Solution: In **Post-deployment conditions**, modify the **Timeout** setting for post-deployment approvals.  
  
Does this achieve the goal?
questions.explanation:
A post-deployment approval occurs after the deployment, whereas the required team-leader approval must be completed before deployment. Its timeout therefore cannot control how long the deployment waits for that required approval. The pre-deployment approval timeout must be set to eight hours; when no approval is granted within that timeout, the deployment is rejected.\
\
**Learn more:** [Control deployments with release approvals - Azure Pipelines](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/release/approvals/approvals?view=azure-devops)

questions.question: You are automating the testing process for your company. You need to automate UI testing of a web application. Which framework should you use?
questions.explanation:
Selenium is a widely used open-source framework designed specifically for automating browser interactions and testing the user interface of web applications. It supports multiple browsers and programming languages, making it the standard tool for web UI test automation. JaCoco is a code coverage tool for Java, Xamarin.UITest is intended for automating UI tests on mobile applications, and Microsoft.CodeAnalysis is an API for source code analysis, none of which are designed for web UI testing.\

The other categories (Navigator, Configuration and Management, Diagnostic Tools) focus on navigating resources, settings changes, or collecting logs/dumps rather than historical availability analysis. **Learn more:** [App Service diagnostics overview](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/app-service/overview-diagnostics)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an Azure subscription that contains the resources shown in the following table.  
  
![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1783721274913-cw6qlgob.png)  
  
Project produces npm packages that are published to Feed1. Feed1 is consumed by multiple projects.  

You need to ensure that only tested packages are available for consumption. The solution must minimize development effort.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Create a feed view named @release and set @release as the default view. After the npm packages test successfully, configure a release pipeline that promotes a package to the @release view.
Create a feed view named @release and set @release as the default view. After the npm packages test successfully, configure a release pipeline that tags the packages as release.
Create a feed view named @default. After the npm packages test successfully, configure a release pipeline that tags the packages as release.
Create a feed view named @default. After the npm packages test successfully, configure a release pipeline that promotes a package to the @default view.

questions.explanation:
Azure Artifacts controls package promotion through feed views, not tags: creating a custom @release view, making it the default view consumers pull from, and having a release pipeline promote a package into @release only after tests pass ensures untested packages remain invisible to consumers while requiring no custom tooling. Azure Artifacts npm feeds have no built-in concept of tagging a package as "release," and the feed's built-in default view is @Local, not a view literally named @default, so C and D describe a nonexistent mechanism.

**Learn more:** [Release views in Azure Artifacts](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/artifacts/concepts/views)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You use release pipelines in Azure Pipelines to deploy an app. Secrets required be the pipeline are stored as pipeline variables. Logging of commands is enabled for the Azure Pipelines agent.  

You need to prevent the values of the secrets from being logged.  

What should you do?

options.text: Store the secrets in the environment variables instead of the pipeline variables.
Pass the secrets on the command line instead of in the pipeline variables.
Apply a prefix of secret to the name of the variables.
Echo the values of the secrets to the command line.

questions.explanation: Azure Pipelines automatically masks recognized secret variable values, but that masking is defeated once a secret is passed as a command-line argument or echoed to output, especially with command logging enabled; there is no naming-prefix convention that triggers masking. Guidance is to never pass secrets on the command line and instead map them into environment variables, which keeps the raw value out of the command text that gets logged.

You have an Azure subscription that contains multiple Azure services.  

You need to send an SMS alert when scheduled maintenance is planned for the Azure services.  

Which two actions should you perform? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.  

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

options.text: Add the user to the Build Administrators group.
Add the user to the Project Administrators group.
From the Security settings of the repository, modify the access control for the user.
From the Security settings of the branch, modify the access control for the user.

questions.explanation:
Branch policies such as requiring a successful build can be overridden by users granted the "Bypass policies when completing pull requests" (or "Bypass policies when pushing") permission. Setting this permission from the branch-level Security settings scopes the exception to only the master branch for only that user, satisfying least privilege. Using the repository-level security would apply the bypass across all branches in the repo, and adding the user to Build Administrators or Project Administrators would grant excessive, unrelated permissions beyond what is needed.

**Learn more:** [Set branch permissions - Azure Repos](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/repos/git/branch-permissions) · [Improve code quality with branch policies - Azure Repos](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/repos/git/branch-policies)

questions.explanation:
By default in Azure DevOps, members of the Readers group can only view and run existing queries — they cannot create or save new ones. Members of the Contributors group, however, can create and save personal ('My Queries') custom work item queries by default, which is exactly what is needed to build reports on project progress. Project Administrators grant broader project-management capabilities (including creating/managing Shared Queries and folders, managing teams, area/iteration paths, repositories, and service endpoints), and Project Collection Administrators grant organization/collection-wide administrative rights across multiple projects — both exceed what is required for simply authoring custom queries. Therefore, adding the project manager to the Contributors group provides the minimum permissions necessary to accomplish the task, in line with the principle of least privilege.

**Learn more:** [Default Permissions Quick Reference - Azure DevOps | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/organizations/security/permissions-access?view=azure-devops) · [Set query permissions in Azure Boards and Azure DevOps - Azure Boards | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/boards/queries/set-query-permissions?view=azure-devops)

You need to perform the GitHub code migration. The solution must support the planned changes for the DevOps environment.  

What should you use?

options.text: an Azure virtual machine scale set

questions.explanation:
Azure Virtual Machine Scale Set agents are self-hosted agents that Azure Pipelines can automatically scale out and in based on job demand. You can configure the number of agents to keep on standby down to 0, so Azure Pipelines only provisions a VM when a pipeline job is queued and removes idle agents after a configurable delay. This elasticity means you avoid paying for compute that sits idle nearly all day, which is ideal for a pipeline that only runs once daily for 30 minutes. This is explicitly the scenario Microsoft documentation calls out: 'You don't want to run dedicated agents around the clock. You want to de-provision agent machines that aren't being used to run jobs.' Standalone Azure VMs would require manual management to avoid idle costs, and AKS/Azure Container Instances are not the natively integrated, cost-optimized self-hosted agent scaling mechanism for this infrequent workload pattern.

**Learn more:** [Azure Virtual Machine Scale Set agents - Azure Pipelines | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/agents/scale-set-agents?view=azure-devops)

You have an Azure solution that includes a build pipeline configured in Azure Pipelines.  
  
You notice that the build pipeline experiences intermittent delays before it starts running.  
  
You need to reduce the time it takes for the build pipeline to start.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Split the build pipeline into multiple stages.

questions.explanation:
Azure Pipelines uses a limited number of parallel jobs (concurrent pipeline runs) per organization. When all available parallel jobs are in use, additional pipeline runs must queue and wait for a slot to free up, which produces intermittent start-up delays that vary with current load. Purchasing an additional parallel job increases the pool's run concurrency, allowing pipelines to start sooner instead of waiting in the queue. This is the documented mitigation from Microsoft's guidance on parallel jobs and pipeline queue times, as opposed to agent pool creation, self-hosted agent enablement (which addresses execution capacity/customization, not necessarily queue wait unless capacity is scaled), or splitting into stages (which restructures the pipeline but doesn't change queue wait time).

**Learn more:** [Parallel jobs in Azure Pipelines](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/licensing/concurrent-jobs)

questions.explanation:
For scenarios where an external (third-party) service or CI tool needs to authenticate against Azure DevOps/Azure Repos—such as to access source code or trigger/report build status—Azure DevOps relies on Personal Access Tokens (PATs). A PAT is a credential that can be generated by a user, is scoped to specific permissions (e.g., Code, Build), and has an expiration date, making it suitable for use by external applications, scripts, and third-party CI/CD tools instead of using the user's full account credentials. This is the documented method described in Microsoft's Azure DevOps authentication guidance for authenticating external tools.

questions.domain: Design and implement build and release pipelines
questions.question:
Your company uses Azure DevOps for the build pipelines and deployment pipelines of Java-based projects.  

You need to recommend a strategy for managing technical debt.

Integrate Azure DevOps and Azure DevTest Labs.

It provides detailed metrics on code smells, vulnerabilities, and maintainability for Java and other languages, making it essential for managing technical debt in Java-based projects. Post-deployment approvals and DevTest Labs do not address technical debt analysis.

questions.domain: Implement an instrumentation strategy
questions.question:
You have a GitHub Enterprise account.  
  
You need to enable push protection for secret scanning of the account repositories.  
  
What should you do first?

options.text: Configure post-deployment approvals in the deployment pipeline.
Configure pre-deployment approvals in the deployment pipeline.
Integrate Azure DevOps and Azure DevTest Labs.

questions.explanation:
Technical debt in Java codebases is tracked using SonarQube's static code analysis, which measures code smells, bugs, vulnerabilities, duplications, and test coverage. Integrating Azure DevOps with SonarQube (via the SonarQube/SonarCloud marketplace extension) adds build tasks such as Prepare Analysis Configuration, Run Code Analysis, and Publish Quality Gate Result, which compute and publish a Quality Gate status for each build. To stop code that carries excessive technical debt from being promoted, that Quality Gate status is checked as a pre-deployment condition/gate on the release pipeline stage — the deployment pauses until the SonarQube Quality Gate check passes (or an approver intervenes), preventing poor-quality code from reaching downstream environments such as Production. Post-deployment approvals occur only after the deployment has already happened and therefore cannot block debt-laden code from being released, and Azure DevTest Labs is used for provisioning test/dev environments and has no role in measuring or gating on code quality/technical debt.

**Learn more:** [Control deployments with release approvals - Azure Pipelines | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/release/approvals/approvals?view=azure-devops) · [Quality gate status in release pipeline | SonarQube Server | Sonar Documentation](https://docs.sonarsource.com/sonarqube-server/devops-platform-integration/azure-devops-integration/adding-analysis-to-pipeline/quality-gate-status-in-release-pipeline)

You need to recommend a Docker container build strategy that satisfies the following requirements:  
  
- Minimizes image sizes  
- Minimizes the security surface area of the final image  
  
What should you include in the recommendation?
questions.explanation:
Multi-stage builds let you use multiple FROM statements in a single Dockerfile, where earlier stages contain build tools, SDKs, and intermediate files, and only the final stage's necessary artifacts (such as compiled binaries) are copied into the final, minimal runtime image. This approach discards unneeded build dependencies and tools from the shipped image, directly reducing both the image size and the attack/security surface area, since fewer packages and tools are present that could be exploited. Docker's official documentation specifically recommends multi-stage builds for this purpose.

**Learn more:** [Multi-stage builds | Docker Docs](https://docs.docker.com/build/building/multi-stage/)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company has a project in Azure DevOps for a new application. The application will be deployed to several Azure virtual machines running Windows Server 2019.  
  
You need to recommend a deployment strategy for the virtual machines that meets the following requirements:  
  
- Ensure that the virtual machines maintain a consistent configuration.  
- Minimize administrative effort required to configure the virtual machines.  
  
What should you include in the recommendation?

options.text: Azure Resource Manager templates and the PowerShell Desired State Configuration (DSC) extension for Windows
Deployment YAML and Azure pipeline deployment groups
Azure Resource Manager templates and the Custom Script Extension for Windows
Deployment YAML and Azure pipeline stage templates

questions.explanation:
PowerShell Desired State Configuration (DSC) provides a declarative, idempotent way to define and enforce the configuration state of Windows machines, automatically correcting drift and maintaining consistency without ongoing manual intervention. Deploying the DSC extension through an Azure Resource Manager template lets the configuration be applied automatically as part of VM provisioning, satisfying both the consistency requirement and the goal of minimizing administrative effort. The Custom Script Extension only executes a script once and does not continuously enforce a desired state, and the YAML pipeline options (deployment groups/stage templates) are release orchestration constructs rather than configuration-state enforcement mechanisms.

**Learn more:** [Desired State Configuration extension with Azure Resource Manager templates - Azure Virtual Machines | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-machines/extensions/dsc-template) · [Azure Desired State Configuration Extension Handler - Azure Virtual Machines | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-machines/extensions/dsc-windows)

questions.domain: Develop a security and compliance plan
questions.question:
Solution: Create an email subscription for an Azure DevOps notification.  
  
Does this satisfy the goal?
questions.explanation:
Email notification subscriptions deliver messages to email recipients, whereas Azure DevOps uses a Jenkins service hook to trigger a Jenkins build when code is pushed to an Azure Repos Git repository. An email subscription therefore does not notify Jenkins as required.\
\
**Learn more:** [Create a service hook for Jenkins - Azure DevOps](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/service-hooks/services/jenkins?view=azure-devops) · [Manage Personal Notification Settings - Azure DevOps](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/organizations/notifications/manage-your-personal-notifications?view=azure-devops)

questions.domain: Design and implement processes and communications
questions.question:
Solution: You add a trigger to the build pipeline.  
  
Does this fulfill the goal?
questions.explanation:
Azure Pipelines triggers cause an Azure Pipelines build to run when a branch receives a push. To trigger Jenkins from a code push in Azure Repos, Azure DevOps requires a Jenkins service hook configured with the code-pushed event and a Jenkins build action.\
\
**Learn more:** [Create a service hook for Jenkins - Azure DevOps](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/service-hooks/services/jenkins?view=azure-devops) · [Specify events that trigger pipelines - Azure Pipelines](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/build/triggers?view=azure-devops)

questions.domain: Design and implement build and release pipelines
questions.question:
Solution: You create a service hook subscription that uses the **Code pushed** event.  
  
Does this satisfy the goal?
questions.explanation:
Azure DevOps service hooks support Jenkins as a consumer, with **Code pushed** as a supported event that can trigger a Jenkins Git or generic build. The event can be filtered to a particular branch, so pushes resulting from developer commits can notify Jenkins.\
\
**Learn more:** [Integrate with service hooks - Azure DevOps](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/service-hooks/overview?view=azure-devops) · [Create a service hook for Jenkins - Azure DevOps](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/service-hooks/services/jenkins?view=azure-devops)

questions.domain: Design and implement build and release pipelines
questions.question:
Solution: Create a service hook subscription that uses the **build completed** event.  
  
Does this satisfy the goal?
questions.explanation:
The **Build completed** event triggers only when an Azure Pipelines build has finished, whereas a developer commit to an Azure Repos branch is handled by the **Code pushed** event. A Jenkins service hook can use Code pushed to trigger Jenkins when repository changes are pushed.\
\
**Learn more:** [Create a service hook for Jenkins](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/service-hooks/services/jenkins?view=azure-devops) · [Service Hook Events - Azure DevOps](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/service-hooks/events?view=azure-devops)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You manage projects by using Azure Boards.  
  
You have a current work item name itemA that is dependant on a work item named itemB.  
  
You need to define the dependency for itemA.  
  
What should you do in the web portal for Azure DevOps?

options.text: Add a Parent link to the user story of itemA.
From Backlogs, open the context menu, select Add link, and then select itemA. Set Link type to Successor and add the ID of itemB.
From itemA, open the Links tab, and then select Add link. Set Link type to References and add the ID of itemB.
From Backlogs, open he context menu, select Add link, and then select itemA. Set Link type to References and add the ID of itemB.

questions.explanation: In Azure DevOps, dependencies are defined using predecessor/successor link types. Since itemA depends on itemB, itemB is the predecessor and itemA is the successor. From Backlogs, select itemA, add a link, set the link type to 'Successor', and reference itemB's ID to establish that itemA succeeds (depends on) itemB.

questions.domain: Design and implement processes and communications
questions.question:
Solution: Set up an Octopus Tentacle on an on-premises computer. Use the Package Application task in the build pipeline.  
  
Does this satisfy the goal?
questions.explanation:
An Octopus Tentacle is used as an Octopus deployment target, whereas build tasks execute on an Azure Pipelines build agent. To access on-premises resources during a build, Azure Pipelines requires a self-hosted agent with connectivity to that environment. In addition, packaging an application does not by itself store the output as an Azure DevOps Server build artifact; a publish-artifact step is required.\
\
**Learn more:** [Azure Pipelines Agents](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/agents/agents?tabs=browser&view=azure-devops) · [Using the Octopus Extension](https://octopus.com/docs/packaging-applications/build-servers/tfs-azure-devops/using-octopus-extension)

questions.domain: Design and implement build and release pipelines
questions.question:
Solution: Set up the build pipeline to use a Hosted Ubuntu agent pool and include the Java Tool Installer task in the build pipeline.  
  
Does this satisfy the goal?
questions.explanation:
Microsoft-hosted agents generally cannot reach on-premises environments behind corporate firewalls. Azure DevOps requires a self-hosted agent with connectivity to the on-premises environment when such access is needed. Installing Java does not establish access to the on-premises dependency-management system.\
\
**Learn more:** [Azure Pipelines agents](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/agents/agents?view=azure-devops)

questions.domain: Design and implement build and release pipelines
questions.question:
Solution: Set up the build pipeline to use a Hosted VS 2019 agent pool. Add the Java Tool Installer task to the build pipeline.  
  
Does this satisfy the goal?
questions.explanation:
Microsoft-hosted Azure Pipelines agents do not have direct access to a corporate on-premises network. A build that must access an on-premises dependency-management system requires a self-hosted agent that has network connectivity to that system. Installing Java does not provide the required network path.\
\
**Learn more:** [Microsoft-hosted agents for Azure Pipelines](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/agents/hosted?view=azure-devops) · [Azure Pipelines agents](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/agents/agents?view=azure-devops)

questions.domain: Design and implement build and release pipelines
questions.question:
Solution: Install and configure a self-hosted build agent on an on-premises computer. Set the build pipeline to use the Default agent pool. Add the Java Tool Installer task to the build pipeline.  
  
Does this meet the goal?
questions.explanation:
A self-hosted Azure Pipelines agent on an on-premises machine has network line of sight to on-premises resources such as a dependency management system, while communicating with Azure DevOps to obtain source from Azure Repos and publish build artifacts. Azure Pipelines supports storing published artifacts in Azure Pipelines rather than copying them to a file share, which satisfies server artifact storage.\
\
**Learn more:** [Azure Pipelines Agents](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/agents/agents?view=azure-devops) · [Publish and download pipeline artifacts](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/artifacts/pipeline-artifacts?view=azure-devops)

questions.domain: Design and implement build and release pipelines
questions.question:
Solution: Configure the build pipeline to use a Microsoft-hosted agent pool running a Linux image. Add the Java Tool Installer task to the build pipeline.  
  
Does this achieve the goal?
questions.explanation:
Microsoft-hosted agents generally do not have line-of-sight connectivity to on-premises environments behind intermediate firewalls. A self-hosted agent with access to the on-premises dependency-management system, or separately configured network access, is required. Installing Java does not provide that connectivity.\
\
**Learn more:** [Azure Pipelines agents](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/agents/agents?view=azure-devops) · [Microsoft-hosted agents for Azure Pipelines](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/agents/hosted?view=azure-devops)

questions.domain: Design and implement build and release pipelines
questions.question:
Solution: Set up the build pipeline to use a Microsoft-hosted agent pool that runs the **Windows Server 2019 with Visual Studio 2019** image. Add the **Java Tool Installer** task to the build pipeline.  
  
Does this satisfy the goal?
questions.explanation:
Microsoft-hosted agent pools do not have direct access to corporate on-premises environments by default. A build that must retrieve dependencies from an on-premises dependency-management system requires an agent with network connectivity to that system, typically a self-hosted agent deployed within or connected to the corporate network. Installing Java does not provide that connectivity.\
\
**Learn more:** [Azure Pipelines Agents](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/agents/agents?tabs=browser&view=azure-devops)

questions.domain: Develop a security and compliance plan
questions.question: Your organization uses Azure Artifacts for managing packages. You need to set up an upstream source in Azure Artifacts specifically for Python packages. Which repository type should you select as the upstream source?
questions.explanation:
Azure Artifacts allows feeds to include upstream sources that proxy public package registries so that packages can be consumed and cached from a single feed. For Python packages, the supported public upstream source type is PyPI (Python Package Index), which is the standard repository for Python packages. npmjs.org is used for npm (JavaScript/Node.js) packages, and Maven Central is used for Java packages, neither of which apply to Python.\
\
**Learn more:** [Use upstream sources - Azure Artifacts](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/artifacts/concepts/upstream-sources)

questions.domain: Implement an instrumentation strategy
questions.question:
You are designing the security validation strategy for a project in Azure DevOps.  

You need to identify package dependencies that have known security issues and can be resolved by an update.  

What should you use?
questions.explanation: SonarQube is a static code analysis platform that scans for security vulnerabilities in code, including identifying package dependencies with known security issues. It integrates into the build pipeline to detect vulnerabilities and provide recommendations for updates. Octopus Deploy is for release management, Jenkins is a CI/CD orchestrator, and Gradle is a build tool—none of which specialize in security vulnerability scanning.

questions.domain: Design and implement a source control strategy
questions.question:
You are designing the security validation strategy for a project in Azure DevOps.  

You need to identify package dependencies that have known security issues and can be resolved by an update.  

What should you use?
questions.explanation:
The CMMI process template in Azure Boards is specifically designed for teams requiring formal change management and an auditable record of decisions. It provides dedicated work item types—Requirement, Change Request, Risk, and Review—that are not present in the Basic, Agile, or Scrum process templates, making it the appropriate choice when a project needs to track requirements, change requests, risks, and reviews.

**Learn more:** [Capability Maturity Model Integration (CMMI) process work item types & workflow - Azure Boards | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/boards/work-items/guidance/cmmi-process-workflow?view=azure-devops) · [Default processes and process templates - Azure Boards | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/boards/work-items/guidance/choose-process?view=azure-devops)

questions.domain: Develop a security and compliance plan
questions.question:
You have an Azure DevOps project named Project1 that references an Azure Artifacts feed named Feed1.  
  
You have a package named Package1 with the versions shown in the following table.  
  
![Question Image](https://cdn.examcademy.com/images/questions/1784203876598-7ygcaapx.png)  
  
You need to build Project1.  
  
Which version of Package1 will be used?
questions.explanation:
Azure Artifacts searches packages published directly to the feed before packages saved from upstream sources and packages available from upstream sources. Therefore, Package1 is resolved from the manually pushed versions in Feed1; the selected version is the latest of those versions, 1.4.0.\
\
**Learn more:** [Azure Artifacts key concepts — Upstream sources](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/artifacts/artifacts-key-concepts?view=azure-devops)

questions.domain: Design and implement processes and communications
questions.question:
You scan a Node.js application using WhiteSource Bolt.  

The scan finds numerous libraries with invalid licenses, but are only used during development.  

You have to make sure that only production dependencies are scanned by WhiteSource Bolt.  

Which of the following is a command you should run?
questions.explanation: Running `npm install --only=prod` (or `--only=production`) installs only production dependencies and excludes development dependencies from the installation. This ensures WhiteSource Bolt scans only production libraries, filtering out development-only licenses and vulnerabilities that are not relevant to the production codebase.

/>","className":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an Azure pipeline that is used to build and deploy an app named App1. The build job uses a Microsoft-hosted Windows agent.

You need to ensure that the build job completes successfully. The solution must minimize administrative effort.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Change the configuration of the build agent.
Change to a Microsoft-hosted Linux agent.

questions.explanation: Private-project Microsoft-hosted pipeline jobs default to a 60-minute timeout unless additional parallel jobs have been purchased, which raises the hard cap to 360 minutes and resolves intermittent timeouts on marginally long-running builds. questions.domain: Design and implement build and release pipelines
questions.question:
You need to configure Azure Pipelines to control App2 builds.  

Which authentication method should you use?
questions.explanation: Personal Access Tokens (PAT) are the recommended authentication method for third-party tools and applications integrating with Azure DevOps. PATs provide a secure, token-based alternative to passwords and can be scoped to specific permissions and timeframes.

questions.domain: Design and implement build and release pipelines
questions.question:
You need to configure Azure Pipelines to control App2 builds.  

Which authentication method should you use?

options.text: Assign the Stakeholder access level to all users.
In Azure DevOps, configure Security in Project Settings.
In Azure AD, configure conditional access.
In Azure AD, configure risky sign-ins.

questions.explanation: Conditional Access in Azure AD allows you to define fine-grained access policies based on device location, network conditions, and other factors. By configuring a conditional access policy to require on-premises network connectivity, you can ensure that only devices connected to your on-premises network can access Azure DevOps, regardless of user identity or access level. This is the primary mechanism in Azure AD for location-based access control.

questions.domain: Design and implement build and release pipelines
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company has multiple microservices-based apps that use the following tracing libraries:  
  
• OpenTelemetry  

• OpenCensus  

• OpenTracing  

• Honeycomb  

• Jaeger  
  
The company purchases an Azure subscription and implements Application Insights in Azure Monitor.  
  
You plan to centralize distributed tracing for the apps.  
  
You need to identify which libraries can integrate directly with Application Insights.  
  
Which two libraries should you identify? Each correct answer presents a complete solution.  
  
NOTE: Each correct solution is worth one point.
questions.explanation: Application Insights supports distributed tracing through both OpenTelemetry and OpenCensus. OpenTelemetry is the vendor-neutral standard for instrumentation, and OpenCensus provides metrics and tracing capabilities. OpenTracing, Jaeger, and Honeycomb do not integrate directly with Application Insights.

questions.domain: Implement an instrumentation strategy
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You plan to deploy a solution that will include multiple microservices.  
  
You need to recommend a deployment strategy for the microservices. The solution must meet the following requirements:  
  
• Enable users to test new features by using a specific URL.  

• Minimize the effort required to promote a test version to production.  

• Minimize the effort required to revert production code to the previous version.  
  
Which strategy should you recommend?
questions.explanation: Blue/green deployment maintains two identical production environments, allowing testers to access the new version via a specific URL before it becomes production. Rollback is as simple as switching traffic back to the blue environment, meeting all three requirements efficiently. A/B testing is for experiments, feature toggles are for feature flags, and progressive exposure is for gradual rollout—none provide the instant, full rollback capability of blue/green.

questions.domain: Design and implement build and release pipelines
questions.question:
You are automating the testing process for your company.  
  
You need to automate UI testing of a web application.  
  
Which framework should you use?
questions.explanation: Playwright is a modern, cross-browser web automation framework developed by Microsoft for automating UI testing across Chrome, Firefox, Safari, and other browsers. It supports multiple programming languages and provides robust element selectors and parallel test execution. JaCoco is for Java code coverage, Xamarin.UITest is for mobile apps, and Microsoft.CodeAnalysis is for static code analysis—none are suitable for web application UI testing.

questions.domain: Develop a security and compliance plan
questions.question:
You are automating the testing process for your company.  
  
You need to automate UI testing of a web application.  
  
Which framework should you use?

options.text: Modify the Integrations options for the pipeline.
Modify the post-deployment conditions for the last stage of the pipeline.
Add an agentless job to the pipeline.
Modify the service hooks for the project.

questions.explanation:
Azure DevOps release pipelines provide an "Integrations" configuration option that, when enabled, automatically reports deployment/release status information to the work items linked to the commits and pull requests included in that release. This is the built-in mechanism for surfacing release details on associated work items, distinct from service hooks (external notifications), post-deployment conditions (approval gates), or agentless jobs (server-side tasks not tied to agents).

**Learn more:** [Add, edit and manage releases - Azure Pipelines](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/release/manage-releases)

questions.domain: Implement an instrumentation strategy
questions.question:
You plan to use Azure DevOps to build and deploy an app that will be hosted in a Kubernetes cluster.  
  
You need to scan the app image for vulnerabilities before the image is deployed to the cluster.  
  
What should you include in the solution?
questions.explanation: Microsoft Defender for Containers provides image vulnerability scanning during the build process before deployment. It scans container images for known vulnerabilities and security misconfigurations, allowing remediation before production deployment to Kubernetes clusters.

questions.domain: Design and implement build and release pipelines
questions.question:
You use Azure Repos to manage source code and Azure Pipelines to implement continuous integration and continuous deployment (CI/CD).  
  
You need to ensure that all comments on pull requests are resolved before the pull requests are included in a build. The solution must minimize administrative effort.  
  
What should you include in the solution?
questions.explanation: Branch policies in Azure Repos enforce quality gates on pull requests, including the requirement that all comments must be resolved before completion. This is a built-in feature that requires minimal configuration and no custom development. Pre-deployment and post-deployment gates apply to release pipelines after PR merge, while custom actions require additional coding.

questions.domain: Implement an instrumentation strategy
questions.question:
You use GitHub for source control.  
  
You are evaluating whether to use proxying to add a private upstream MyGet package feed to your MyGet feed.  
  
What are two possible advantages of this approach? Each correct answer presents a complete solution.  
  
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

options.text: minimizes the impact of upstream source availability issues
minimizes latency when accessing the package
minimizes the impact on your storage quota

questions.explanation: Proxying an upstream MyGet feed lets your feed authenticate against the private upstream automatically on the consumer's behalf, so users don't need separate credentials for it, and packages pulled through the proxy from the upstream do not count toward your own feed's storage quota. **Learn more:** [MyGet upstream sources](https://docs.myget.org/docs/reference/upstream-sources)

questions.domain: Design and implement build and release pipelines
questions.question:
Solution: You recommend defining a container job that uses a custom container with the JavaScript packages preinstalled.  
  
Does this achieve the goal?
questions.explanation:
Azure Pipelines checks source code out into the job workspace at runtime, while a container job merely supplies the execution environment. Packages baked into a custom container image do not automatically become the checked-out React application's dependencies, so this approach does not avoid installing the npm packages for that workspace. A dependency cache is needed to reduce repeated npm installation time.\
\
**Learn more:** [YAML pipeline container jobs - Azure Pipelines](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/process/container-phases?view=azure-devops) · [Check out multiple repositories in your pipeline - Azure Pipelines](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/repos/multi-repo-checkout?view=azure-devops)

questions.domain: Design and implement build and release pipelines
questions.question:
Solution: You recommend that parallel jobs be enabled for the pipeline.  
  
Does this achieve the goal?
questions.explanation:
Parallel-job capacity runs separate pipeline jobs concurrently; it does not reduce the npm installation time in a pipeline that contains only one job. Caching npm dependencies between pipeline runs is the Azure Pipelines mechanism intended to reduce repeated package-download time.\
\
**Learn more:** [Pipeline caching - Azure Pipelines](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/release/caching?view=azure-devops) · [Jobs in Azure Pipelines](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/process/phases?view=azure-devops)

questions.domain: Design and implement build and release pipelines
questions.question:
Solution: You recommend that pipeline caching be enabled.  
  
Does this achieve the goal?
questions.explanation:
Azure Pipelines caching stores dependency files between runs, improving build performance. For Node.js projects, Microsoft recommends caching npm’s shared cache directory so package installation can reuse downloaded packages rather than downloading them again on every pipeline run.\
\
**Learn more:** [Pipeline caching - Azure Pipelines](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/release/caching?view=azure-devops) · [Cache@2 - Cache v2 task](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/tasks/reference/cache-v2?view=azure-pipelines)

questions.domain: Design and implement build and release pipelines
questions.question:
Solution: You recommend using pipeline artifacts.  
  
Does this achieve the goal?
questions.explanation: Pipeline artifacts are designed to publish and download files between jobs or stages. They do not provide a reusable dependency cache across pipeline runs, and a pipeline with a single job has no separate job that needs the artifact. Caching npm dependencies is the mechanism that reduces repeated package-installation time.

questions.domain: Develop a security and compliance plan
questions.question:
Solution: You recommend using pipeline artifacts.  
  
Does this achieve the goal?

options.text: a pre-deployment task that runs a security and compliance assessment
a post-deployment task that runs a security and compliance assessment
an ARM template deployment task to assign Policy1 to Subscription1
an ARM template deployment task to deploy Policy1 to Subscription1

questions.explanation: Because Policy1 has an audit effect rather than a deny effect, it does not block a non-compliant resource from being created; it only records the resource's compliance state after Azure Policy evaluates it, which happens once the deployment already exists. A post-deployment task that runs a compliance assessment is therefore what lets Pipeline1 confirm whether the resources it just deployed actually satisfy Policy1.

You have an Azure Resource Manager template that deploys a multi-tier application. You need to prevent the user who performs the deployment from viewing the account credentials and connection strings used by the application. What should you use?

options.text: an Azure Resource Manager parameter file

questions.explanation:
Azure Key Vault allows you to store secrets, such as account credentials and connection strings, and reference them in an ARM template parameter file using a static or dynamic Key Vault reference. When a parameter references a Key Vault secret, Azure Resource Manager retrieves the secret value securely at deployment time without exposing it in the template, deployment outputs, or deployment history to the person performing the deployment—unless that person is separately granted access to read the secret from the vault. This ensures credentials remain hidden from the deployer while still being usable by the deployment process. Configuration files like Web.config or appsettings.json store secrets in plaintext within the application, offering no protection against a deploying user viewing them, and Azure Storage tables and plain ARM parameter files (without Key Vault integration) also do not provide this secret-hiding capability.

**Learn more:** [Use Azure Key Vault to pass secure parameter value during deployment](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-resource-manager/templates/key-vault-parameter?tabs=azure-cli)

questions.domain: Design and implement build and release pipelines
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have configured an availability test in Azure Application Insights. You need to send an email notification to your company's customer services department whenever availability becomes degraded. To handle the email and any follow-up actions, you create an Azure logic app.  
  
Which type of trigger should you use to invoke the logic app?
questions.explanation:
Azure Monitor alerts (including Application Insights availability alerts) invoke a Logic App through an action group configured with the 'Logic App' action type. The Logic App itself must begin with the built-in 'When a HTTP request is received' trigger, which creates an endpoint URL that the alert engine calls with the alert payload. In the Logic App's underlying workflow definition, this trigger's type is 'Request' (kind: Http), making it the correct trigger to select — as documented in Microsoft's guidance on customizing alert notifications with Logic Apps.

**Learn more:** [Customize alert notifications by using Logic Apps - Azure Monitor | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-monitor/alerts/alerts-logic-apps)

questions.domain: Develop a security and compliance plan
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],While reviewing code, you find quality issues in a Java application.  
  
You need to recommend a solution that can detect quality issues such as:  
  
- Unused variables  
- Empty catch blocks  
  
What should you recommend?

options.text: In a Maven build task, select Run PMD.
In an Xcode build task, select Use xcpretty from Advanced.
In a Gulp build task, specify a custom condition expression.
In a Grunt build task, select Enabled from Control Options.

questions.explanation:
PMD is a source code analyzer for Java that finds common programming flaws such as unused variables, unused imports, empty catch blocks, and unnecessary object creation. In a Maven build task (such as in Azure Pipelines), selecting the 'Run PMD' option enables this static analysis as part of the build, allowing these specific quality issues to be detected automatically.

**Learn more:** [Maven task - Azure Pipelines](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/tasks/reference/maven-v3) · [PMD - An extensible cross-language static code analyzer](https://pmd.github.io/)

questions.domain: Implement an instrumentation strategy
questions.question:
You have a GitHub repository.  
  
You need to create a tag named v3.0.5 and ensure that the tag is available in the remote repository.  
  
Which two commands should you run? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.  
  
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.
questions.explanation: Creating and pushing a tag requires two commands: first, git tag v3.0.5 creates the tag locally, then git push origin v3.0.5 pushes it to the remote repository. These two commands together accomplish the full objective. The other options do not create tags (A is for cleanup, D is for commits, E is for staging).
