lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company is building an iOS application, and every user of the app has a device that belongs to a private distribution group configured in Microsoft Visual Studio App Center.  
  
You are preparing to distribute a new release of the app through App Center.  
  
You need to determine which certificate file you must upload to App Center in order to distribute this new release.  
  
Which file type should you upload to App Center?
questions.explanation:
App Center's iOS distribution and device auto-provisioning process re-signs the app for devices registered in the distribution group, which requires the distribution certificate along with its private key. On macOS this certificate and key pair is exported from Keychain Access as a PKCS#12 container using the .p12 file extension, which is the file type App Center requires you to upload for iOS release management. A .cer file contains only the public certificate without the private key, .pfx is the Windows-style PKCS#12 extension not used in the Apple ecosystem, and .pvk is a separate private-key file format used with Microsoft's code-signing tools, none of which App Center accepts for this purpose.

**Learn more:** [Device registration - Visual Studio App Center | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/appcenter/distribution/auto-provisioning)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are building a pipeline in Azure Pipelines. Several of the tests you have defined may fail because of the third-party applications they depend on. You need to make sure the build pipeline still completes successfully even when those third-party applications are unavailable.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Configure the build pipeline to use parallel jobs
Add the Requirements quality widget to your dashboard

questions.explanation:
Azure DevOps provides a flaky test management feature (enabled under Project Settings > Test management) specifically to handle tests that produce inconsistent pass/fail results due to factors outside the code itself, such as unreliable or unavailable third-party dependencies. Once a test is detected or manually marked as flaky, you can configure the flaky test options so that flaky test failures are excluded from the test summary/pass percentage and the failure is suppressed, allowing the overall pipeline to complete successfully instead of being marked as failed. This directly addresses failures caused by third-party application unavailability, unlike parallel jobs (which only affects execution speed/concurrency), raising the pass percentage threshold (which is a blunt, pipeline-wide tolerance setting not tied to identifying specific unreliable tests), or the Requirements quality dashboard widget (a reporting visualization with no effect on pipeline outcome).

**Learn more:** [Manage flaky tests - Azure Pipelines | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/test/flaky-test-management?view=azure-devops) · [Review test results - Azure Pipelines | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/test/review-continuous-test-results-after-build?view=azure-devops)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You manage projects by using Azure Boards and manage project code by using GitHub.

You need to link work item 123 to a new pull request.  
  
What are two ways to accomplish this goal? Each correct answer provides a complete solution.

options.text: In the Development section for work item 123, select Add link, and then enter the URL of the pull request.
To the description of the pull request, add #AB123.
To work item 123 add a comment that includes the URL of the pull request.

questions.explanation:

You receive crash reports from Crashlytics.  

You need to capture the following data:

Configure the Crashlytics pod in the app.
Import the Firebase module to UIApplicationDelegate.

questions.explanation: Firebase Crashlytics requires both the Crashlytics SDK and Google Analytics integration to capture crash-free users, breadcrumbs, and custom events. • Support granting privileges to the identity.  
  
Which type of identity should you use?
questions.explanation: User-assigned managed identity is a standalone Azure resource that can be assigned to multiple Azure resources (VMs), allowing them to share a single identity with automatic credential management. System-assigned managed identities can only be associated with one resource. For four VMs to use a single managed identity, you must use a user-assigned managed identity, which also supports role-based access control for privilege management.

questions.domain: Develop a security and compliance plan
questions.question:
You have an Azure Pipelines pipeline named Pipeline1 and a user named User1. Pipeline1 contains a temporary final stage named final1.  
  
You need to ensure that User1 can delete final1 when testing is complete. The solution must follow the principle of least privilege.  
  
At which level should you grant permissions to User1?
questions.explanation:
Azure DevOps lets you secure an individual pipeline stage independently from the rest of the pipeline, so you can grant User1 rights scoped only to the final1 stage instead of the entire pipeline, project, or organization. This satisfies least privilege because User1 gains no ability to modify or delete anything outside that one stage.\
\
**Learn more:** [Set release and release stage permissions](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/policies/permissions?view=azure-devops#set-release-stage-permissions)

questions.explanation: Analytics features in monitoring tools parse logs from multiple sources, correlate events, and identify root causes of pipeline failures. Synthetic monitoring tests service availability; alert management handles notifications; directed monitoring is not a standard monitoring feature for root cause analysis.

questions.question:
You have an Azure subscription.  
  
You create two Bicep templates named Template1 and Template2 that will be used to create a virtual machine and a website.  
  
You need to create a template named Template3 that will reuse logic from Template1 and Template2.  
  
What should you define first?
questions.explanation:
Deployment gates in Azure Pipelines let you add automated checks (such as a call to an Azure Function, Azure Monitor alert, or REST API) that must succeed before a release is allowed to proceed to a stage. By configuring a gate that queries Azure Policy compliance status for the target resources, you can block a release from being deployed until it satisfies the Azure Policy rules assigned to Sub1. Deployment queue settings only control how concurrent releases are queued, deployment triggers control when a release is created/started, and pipeline variables merely store configuration values—none of these enforce policy compliance checks before deployment.

**Learn more:** [Release deployment control using approvals and gates - Azure Pipelines](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/release/approvals/gates)

questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are designing an Azure DevOps strategy for your company's development team. You suspect that the team's productivity is low because of accumulated technical debt. You need to recommend a metric to assess the amount of the team's technical debt. What should you recommend?

options.text: the number of code modules in an application
the number of unit test failures
the percentage of unit test failures
the percentage of overall time spent on rework

questions.explanation: Technical debt accumulates when quick, less-than-ideal solutions are chosen over time, requiring future rework to fix or improve. The percentage of overall time a team spends on rework (as opposed to building new functionality) directly reflects how much technical debt is dragging on productivity, making it the appropriate metric for assessing technical debt. Metrics like module count or unit test failure rates measure code size or current defect/build quality rather than the burden of historical shortcuts that constitute technical debt.

The task uses `condition: always()`, which runs the step even when the pipeline run is cancelled — the requirement is that tests run for every run *unless* it is cancelled, which is what `succeededOrFailed()` expresses. - Beta releases are distributed to your testers.  
- User feedback on the functionality of new app features is gathered.  
  
Which of the following must be included as part of your solution?
questions.explanation: The Microsoft Test & Feedback extension integrates with Azure DevOps to enable exploratory testing, crash report collection (as structured work items), beta distribution coordination, and user feedback gathering. While Visual Studio App Center is an alternative for mobile-focused scenarios, the Test & Feedback extension meets all stated requirements through integration with Azure DevOps. questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You manage a build pipeline in Azure Pipelines that occasionally fails. You determine that a test which measures the response time of an API endpoint is the cause of these failures. You need to stop the build pipeline from failing because of this test.  
  
Which two actions should you take? Each correct answer presents part of the solution. (Choose two.)  
  
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

options.text: Set Flaky test detection to Off.
Clear Flaky tests included in test pass percentage.
Manually mark the test as flaky.

questions.explanation:
Azure Pipelines' flaky test management feature allows a specific test to be manually flagged as flaky, after which Azure DevOps continues to treat it as flaky on future runs until it is unmarked. Separately, under Flaky test options, clearing 'Flaky tests included in test pass percentage' removes both passed and failed results of flaky tests from the pass-percentage calculation (they instead appear under 'Tests not reported'), which prevents an intermittent failure in that test from failing the build. Disabling flaky test detection altogether would eliminate this management capability and cause every failure of the test to count as a real failure. Test Impact Analysis only limits which tests run based on code changes, and test slicing only partitions tests for parallel execution — neither affects how flaky failures are counted toward pipeline success or failure.

**Learn more:** [Manage flaky tests - Azure Pipelines | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/test/flaky-test-management?view=azure-devops) · [Use Test Impact Analysis - Azure Pipelines | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/test/test-impact-analysis?view=azure-devops)

questions.domain: Design and implement build and release pipelines

options.text: You should make use of static code analysis.
You should make use of views.
You should make use of dynamic code analysis.
You should make use of upstream sources.

questions.explanation:
Azure Artifacts feeds support the concept of views (such as @Local, @Prerelease, and @Release), which let you promote a package through different stages within a single feed. By publishing all builds to the same feed but only exposing packages that have passed validation to a release view, you can control which package versions are visible to consumers, effectively restricting in-development packages from being released while still allowing multiple builds to share one feed. Upstream sources instead allow a feed to pull packages from other feeds or public registries and do not address restricting release visibility of packages within your own feed.

**Learn more:** [Views in Azure Artifacts feeds](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/artifacts/concepts/views)

options.text: Service Map in Azure Log Analytics
availability tests in Azure Application Insights
Application Map in Azure Application Insights

questions.explanation:
Availability tests in Azure Application Insights allow you to configure synthetic tests (such as URL ping tests) that periodically send requests to your web app endpoint from multiple geographic locations and verify that it returns a successful HTTP status code (200) within an expected response time. When the test fails—such as when a non-200 status code is returned—Application Insights raises an availability alert, which can be configured with an action group to send an email notification to the DevOps team. Service Map and Application Map are used for visualizing application component dependencies and diagnosing performance/failure correlations, not for synthetic endpoint status monitoring, and Profiler is used for capturing detailed code-level performance traces of live requests, not availability checks.

**Learn more:** [Monitor the availability of any website - Azure Monitor | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-monitor/app/availability-overview)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an existing build pipeline configured in Azure Pipelines.  
  
You need to enable incremental builds so that the environment is not purged between pipeline executions.  
  
What should you use?
questions.explanation:
A self-hosted agent is a machine you set up and maintain yourself to run pipeline jobs. Unlike Microsoft-hosted agents, which provision a fresh virtual machine for every job and discard it afterward, a self-hosted agent retains its working directories between runs by default (only the artifact staging directory and test results directory are cleaned). This persistence lets build tools reuse existing files and intermediate outputs, enabling incremental builds and deployments across pipeline executions without purging the environment each time.

**Learn more:** [Azure Pipelines Agents - Azure Pipelines | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/agents/agents?view=azure-devops) · [Microsoft-hosted agents for Azure Pipelines - Azure Pipelines | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/agents/hosted?view=azure-devops)

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an Azure DevOps organization named Contoso and an Azure subscription. The subscription includes an Azure virtual machine scale set named VMSS1 and an Azure Standard Load Balancer named LB1, where LB1 distributes incoming requests across the VMSS1 instances.  
  
You use Azure DevOps to build a web app named App1 and deploy it to VMSS1. App1 is accessible only over HTTPS and is configured to require mutual authentication using a client certificate.  
  
You need to recommend a solution for implementing a health check for App1 that meets the following requirements:  
  
- Identifies whether individual VMSS1 instances are eligible for an upgrade operation.  
- Minimizes administrative effort.  
  
What should you include in the recommendation?

options.text: an Azure Load Balancer health probe

questions.explanation:
The Application Health extension runs on each virtual machine scale set instance and probes a specified application endpoint (using TCP, HTTP, or HTTPS), reporting the application's health status back to the Azure platform. Azure uses this health signal natively to determine whether an instance is healthy and eligible for upgrade operations (as well as for automatic instance repairs), without requiring custom scripting or manual health-check logic. In contrast, a Load Balancer health probe only informs load-balancing traffic decisions and is not designed to signal per-instance upgrade eligibility to the scale set's orchestration, Azure Monitor autoscale addresses scaling rather than upgrade health, and the Custom Script Extension would require building and maintaining custom health-check code, increasing administrative overhead.

**Learn more:** [Use Application Health extension with Azure Virtual Machine Scale Sets](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-machine-scale-sets/virtual-machine-scale-sets-health-extension) · [Automatic OS image upgrades with Azure Virtual Machine Scale Sets](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-machine-scale-sets/virtual-machine-scale-sets-automatic-upgrade)

questions.explanation:
Pre-deployment gates control whether a release can proceed to deployment by evaluating configured conditions at the release stage. They do not provide ongoing detection of license violations or prohibited software libraries during development; dependency and license scanning must be integrated into the development or build workflow.\
\
**Learn more:** [Deployment gates concepts - Azure Pipelines](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/release/approvals/gates?view=azure-devops)

questions.explanation:
Continuous deployment automates releasing validated updates to production; it does not detect licensing violations or prohibited libraries. Component Governance for CI/CD provides open-source component license-compliance checks and policy enforcement.\
\
**Learn more:** [Make your Azure DevOps secure](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/organizations/security/security-overview?view=azure-devops) · [Get Started with DevOps Architecture Design](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/guide/devops/devops-get-started)

questions.question:
Solution: You implement continuous deployment.  
  
Does this satisfy the goal?

options.text: Configure the pipelines to use the Microsoft-hosted agents.

questions.explanation:
Because the pipelines must access files on an on-premises file system, they must continue running on self-hosted agents rather than Microsoft-hosted agents. In Azure DevOps, the number of jobs that can execute simultaneously is governed by the number of parallel jobs (parallelism slots) an organization has, not by the number of agents registered in a pool. A free-tier organization is granted only one free self-hosted parallel job, so even with five agents available, only one job runs at a time while the rest queue. Adding more self-hosted agents would not change this limit, since the agents would still be constrained to the single available parallel job slot. Purchasing additional self-hosted parallel jobs increases the number of jobs that can run concurrently across the existing agent pool, directly reducing queuing and overall build time.

**Learn more:** [Configure and pay for parallel jobs - Azure DevOps | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/licensing/concurrent-jobs?view=azure-devops)

lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an Azure DevOps project that produces Node Package Manager (npm) packages. Multiple projects consume the packages.  

You need to configure Azure Artifacts to ensure that both the latest and pre-release versions of the packages are available for consumption.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Create two feed views named @prerelease and @release, Set @release as the default view. Configure a release pipeline that tags the packages as release after successful testing.
Create a feed view named @prerelease. Configure a release pipeline that tags the packages as release after successful testing.
Create two feed views named @prerelease and @default. Configure a release pipeline that promotes a package to the @default view after successful testing.
Create two feed views named @prerelease and @release. Set @release as the default view. Configure a release pipeline that promotes a package to the @release view after successful testing.

questions.explanation: Azure Artifacts manages npm package visibility through feed views. Creating separate @prerelease and @release views, setting @release as default, and using promotion (not tagging) allows both latest stable and pre-release versions to be available to consumers. Promoting packages between views is the recommended approach.

questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company builds a multi-tier web application. You use Azure DevOps and host the production application on Azure virtual machines. Your team prepares an Azure Resource Manager template of the virtual machine that will be used to test new features.  
  
You need to create a staging environment in Azure that meets the following requirements:  
  
- Minimizes the cost of Azure hosting  
- Provisions the virtual machines automatically  
- Uses the custom Azure Resource Manager template to provision the virtual machines  
  
What should you do?

options.text: In Azure Cloud Shell, run Azure CLI commands to create and delete the new virtual machines in a staging resource group.
In Azure DevOps, configure new tasks in the release pipeline to deploy to Azure Cloud Services.
From Azure Cloud Shell, run Azure PowerShell commands to create and delete the new virtual machines in a staging resource group.
In Azure DevOps, configure new tasks in the release pipeline to create and delete the virtual machines in Azure DevTest Labs.

questions.explanation:
Azure DevTest Labs is purpose-built for creating on-demand, cost-controlled test/staging environments. It supports provisioning VMs from custom ARM templates, and Azure DevOps release pipelines include dedicated DevTest Labs tasks to automatically create and delete VMs as part of a release. DevTest Labs also provides cost-management features such as auto-shutdown and auto-start policies, quotas, and formulas that minimize hosting costs. Running ad hoc CLI or PowerShell commands from Cloud Shell does not provide automated, pipeline-integrated provisioning tied to release stages, and Azure Cloud Services is an unrelated PaaS compute offering not suited for VM-based ARM template deployments.

**Learn more:** [Add a VM to Azure DevTest Labs by using Azure Pipelines](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devtest-labs/use-devtest-labs-build-release-pipelines) · [Azure DevTest Labs documentation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devtest-labs/devtest-lab-overview)

Enable GitHub annotations for the board.
Install the Azure Boards app for GitHub.
Select Allow anonymous users to access the status badge.

questions.explanation:
Azure Boards status badges are added by copying board-generated Markdown into a GitHub repository’s `README.md`. The Azure DevOps project must first be connected to that GitHub repository; installing and authorizing the Azure Boards app establishes that integration. Anonymous access is only an optional badge setting, while a personal access token and GitHub annotations are unnecessary for this purpose.

**Learn more:** [Install the Azure Boards app for GitHub](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/boards/github/install-github-app?view=azure-devops) · [Add status badges for your GitHub repo](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/boards/github/configure-status-badges?view=azure-devops)

questions.domain: Design and implement processes and communications
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You need to evaluate whether the underlined portion of the statement below is correct.  
  
The Burnup widget measures the elapsed time from creation of work items to their completion.  
  
Select **No adjustment required** if the underlined segment is accurate. If it is not accurate, select the choice that correctly replaces it.
questions.explanation:
In Azure DevOps, the Burnup widget tracks completed work against total scope over a period of time (useful for release burnups, bug burnups, etc.), not the time elapsed per work item. The metric that specifically measures the elapsed time from when a work item is created until it is closed is called Lead Time. Because the description in the statement matches Lead Time rather than Burnup, the underlined segment should be corrected to 'Lead time'.

**Learn more:** [Burndown and burnup guidance - Azure DevOps | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/report/dashboards/burndown-guidance?view=azure-devops) · [Cumulative Flow Guidance - Azure DevOps | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/report/dashboards/cumulative-flow-cycle-lead-time-guidance?view=azure-devops)

questions.domain: Design and implement processes and communications
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are designing a strategy to monitor baseline metrics for Azure virtual machines running Windows Server.  
  
You need to collect detailed data about the processes running inside the guest operating system.  
  
Which two agents should you deploy? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.  
  
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

options.text: the Azure Network Watcher Agent for Windows

questions.explanation:
VM insights' Map feature, which shows detailed process and dependency information running inside a VM's guest OS, requires both the Log Analytics agent (to collect and forward monitoring data to a Log Analytics workspace) and the Dependency agent (which discovers processes and their inter-process/network connections and passes that data through the Log Analytics agent). Neither agent alone provides this capability - the Dependency agent has no independent data channel and depends on the Log Analytics agent being installed on the same VM. The Telegraf agent is used to send custom metrics to Azure Monitor Metrics, not process-level guest data, and the Network Watcher agent handles network diagnostics such as packet capture and flow logs rather than process monitoring.

**Learn more:** [Overview of the Dependency Agent](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-monitor/vm/vminsights-dependency-agent-maintenance) · [Enable VM insights overview](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-monitor/vm/vminsights-enable-overview)

questions.domain: Implement an instrumentation strategy
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your team follows an agile development approach.  
  
You need to recommend a branching strategy for the team's Git repository. The strategy must meet the following requirements:  
  
- Provide the ability to work on multiple independent tasks in parallel.  
- Ensure that checked-in code remains in a releasable state at all times.  
- Ensure that new features can be abandoned at any time.  
- Encourage experimentation.  
  
What should you recommend?

options.text: a single long-running branch without forking
a single fork per team member
a single long-running branch with multiple short-lived feature branches

questions.explanation:
A trunk-based approach that uses one long-running main branch together with multiple short-lived feature branches satisfies all of the stated requirements. Each task or feature is developed in its own short-lived branch, allowing several tasks to proceed in parallel without interfering with one another. Because the main branch only receives completed, reviewed, and tested work through merges, it remains in a releasable state at all times. Since each feature lives in its own isolated branch, that branch (and the feature) can be abandoned or deleted at any point without affecting the main branch or other in-progress work. The isolation also encourages experimentation, since developers can try out changes in a disposable branch without risk to the stable codebase. This is the branching model recommended in Microsoft's Azure Repos/Azure DevOps guidance for agile teams, as opposed to a single branch with no forking (no isolation), multiple long-running branches (integration and merge complexity, harder to keep releasable), or one fork per team member (oriented toward distributed/open-source contribution workflows rather than rapid, releasable agile delivery).

**Learn more:** [Adopt a Git branching strategy - Azure Repos](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/repos/git/git-branching-guidance)

questions.domain: Design and implement build and release pipelines
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company intends to adopt an agile approach to software development.  
  
You need to recommend an application that will enable communication among development team members located around the world. The application must meet the following requirements:  
  
- Allow members of different project teams to be isolated into separate communication channels, while retaining a history of the chats within those channels.  
- Be available on Windows 10, Mac OS, iOS, and Android.  
- Allow external contractors and suppliers to be added to projects.  
- Integrate directly with Azure DevOps.  
  
What should you recommend?
questions.explanation:
Microsoft Teams provides channel-based communication with persistent chat history for isolating project teams, runs natively on Windows 10, macOS, iOS, and Android, supports guest access so external contractors and suppliers can be added to a team, and has a first-party integration (the Azure Boards app) that connects directly with Azure DevOps for work item and notification integration. Microsoft Project is a project-management/scheduling tool, not a communications platform; Bamboo is Atlassian's CI/CD build tool with no Azure DevOps integration; and Microsoft Lync (Skype for Business) lacks the persistent channel history and native Azure DevOps integration that Teams offers.

**Learn more:** [Azure Boards app for Microsoft Teams](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/boards/integrations/azure-boards-app-microsoft-teams) · [Add guests to a team in Microsoft Teams](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoftteams/guest-access)

questions.domain: Design and implement build and release pipelines
questions.explanation:
Static code analysis tools are designed to inspect source code automatically without executing it, and they are most effective when integrated directly into the build process (e.g., as a build step in a CI/CD pipeline). This ensures that every code change is analyzed for quality, style, and potential defects as soon as it is compiled, allowing issues to be caught and addressed immediately—before the code advances to integration testing, staging, or production release. Embedding static analysis in the build phase creates fast, continuous feedback for developers, which directly addresses code quality problems caused by time pressure, since issues are surfaced early rather than discovered later in the release pipeline.

**Learn more:** [Azure Pipelines - Configure code analysis](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/apps/aspnet/build-aspnet-4) · [SonarQube integration with Azure DevOps](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/ecosystems/sonarqube)

questions.domain: Design and implement build and release pipelines
questions.question:
You are configuring project metrics for dashboards in Azure DevOps.  

You need to configure a chart widget that measures the elapsed time to complete work items once they become active.  

Which of the following is the widget you should use?
questions.explanation: Cycle time is a metric that specifically measures the elapsed time from when a work item transitions to an active state until it is completed. It directly reflects the time between activation and closure. Cumulative Flow Diagram shows state counts over time, Burnup shows completed work, and Burndown shows remaining work—none measure elapsed time per item.

questions.domain: Design and implement build and release pipelines
questions.question:
You are configuring project metrics for dashboards in Azure DevOps.  

You need to configure a chart widget that measures the elapsed time to complete work items once they become active.  

Which of the following is the widget you should use?
questions.explanation:
Slack meets all the stated requirements: it provides channel-based communication that isolates project teams while retaining searchable chat history, it runs natively on Windows 10, macOS, iOS, and Android, it allows external users such as contractors and suppliers to be invited as guests to specific channels, and it offers a direct integration with Azure DevOps (via the Azure Boards app for Slack) to post work item and pipeline notifications into channels. Skype for Business does not provide the same persistent, isolated channel-based history model or native Azure DevOps integration. Bamboo and Octopus are continuous integration/deployment tools, not team communication platforms, so they do not satisfy the requirement at all.

**Learn more:** [Azure Boards for Slack](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/boards/integrations/slack-tutorial)

questions.domain: Implement an instrumentation strategy
questions.question:
Solution: Create a main template that deploys the resources in one resource group and a nested template that deploys the resources in the other resource group.  
  
Does this meet the goal?
questions.explanation:
An ARM template can deploy to multiple resource groups by placing resources for the deployment’s target resource group in the main template and using a nested deployment targeted to the other resource group. The nested deployment specifies the destination resource group, allowing the virtual machines and SQL databases to be deployed to their respective groups.\
\
**Learn more:** [Use Azure Resource Manager templates to deploy resources to resource groups](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-resource-manager/templates/deploy-to-resource-group)

questions.domain: Design and implement processes and communications
questions.question:
Solution: Create a main template containing two linked templates, with each template deploying the resources in its corresponding group.  
  
Does this satisfy the goal?
questions.explanation:
A subscription-level ARM template can create the two resource groups and use linked deployments targeted at those resource groups. Linked templates support deploying resources to multiple resource groups in a single deployment, so separate linked templates can deploy the virtual machines and Azure SQL databases to their respective groups.\
\
**Learn more:** [Use Azure Resource Manager templates to deploy resources to resource groups](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-resource-manager/templates/deploy-to-resource-group)

questions.domain: Design and implement processes and communications
questions.question:
Solution: Create two standalone templates, each of which deploys the resources in its respective group.  
  
Does this meet the goal?
questions.explanation:
Resource-group-scoped ARM template deployments require the target resource group to exist. Creating resource groups requires a subscription-scope deployment; resources can then be deployed to those groups through nested or linked templates. Two standalone templates that only deploy resources into their respective groups do not create the two required resource groups.\
\
**Learn more:** [Deploy resources to subscription - Azure Resource Manager](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-resource-manager/templates/deploy-to-subscription)

questions.domain: Design and implement processes and communications
questions.question:
Solution: Create one standalone template to deploy all of the resources.  
  
Does this achieve the goal?
questions.explanation:
Resources targeted at more than one resource group require deployments scoped to those groups, using nested or linked templates to target an additional resource group. A single standalone deployment template does not provide those separate resource-group scopes.\
\
**Learn more:** [Use Azure Resource Manager templates to deploy resources to resource groups](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-resource-manager/templates/deploy-to-resource-group)

questions.domain: Design and implement build and release pipelines
questions.question:
You need to meet the technical requirements for controlling access to Azure DevOps.  

What should you use?

options.text: conditional access policies in Azure AD

questions.explanation: Azure AD Conditional Access policies enable location-based and IP-based access control to Azure DevOps. This allows you to restrict access based on network location or geography. MFA, RBAC, and firewalls do not directly address location-based access requirements.

Which feature should be used to enforce the code quality restriction on the release pipeline for the investment planning applications suite?
questions.explanation:
Deployment gates in Azure Pipelines are automated checks configured as pre-deployment or post-deployment conditions on a release stage. They query external services or pipeline metrics—such as code coverage, pass rate, or other quality signals—and only allow the release to proceed to the next stage if those metrics meet a predefined threshold. This makes gates the appropriate mechanism for enforcing an objective, automated code quality restriction, as opposed to approvals (pre- or post-deployment), which require manual human sign-off, or triggers, which simply initiate pipeline execution based on events like commits or schedules.

**Learn more:** [Deployment gates concepts - Azure Pipelines | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/release/approvals/gates?view=azure-devops)

You use Azure Pipelines to manage build pipelines, GitHub to store source code, and Dependabot to manage dependencies.  
  
You have an app named App1. Dependabot detects a dependency in App1 that requires an update.  
  
What should you do first to apply the update?
questions.explanation:
Dependabot automatically scans a repository's dependency files, and when it finds an outdated or vulnerable dependency it creates a new branch with the required version change and opens a pull request for that change on its own — no manual branch creation or PR creation is needed. The engineer's first required action to move the update forward is to review and approve that automatically generated pull request, after which the associated Azure Pipelines build can validate the change and it can be merged/committed.

**Learn more:** [Dependabot quickstart guide - GitHub Docs](https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/getting-started/dependabot-quickstart-guide) · [Exam AZ-400 topic 3 question 19 discussion - ExamTopics](https://www.examtopics.com/discussions/microsoft/view/36309-exam-az-400-topic-3-question-19-discussion/)

questions.domain: Design and implement processes and communications
questions.explanation:
Microsoft-hosted agents offer a set of predefined VM images, each identified by an image name that you specify in the pool.vmImage property of a YAML pipeline. To build and host container images containing the full .NET Framework, a Windows-based image with the appropriate Windows Server/Windows 10 base and Docker tooling is required. The 'vs2017-win2016' image (Windows Server 2016 with Visual Studio 2017 and Docker support) and the 'win1803' image (Windows 10 version 1803) are both valid Microsoft-hosted images suited for building full .NET Framework container images. Linux (ubuntu-16.04) and macOS (macOS-10.13) images cannot run or build full .NET Framework Windows containers, and 'vs.2015-win2012r2' is not offered/suitable for this container-build scenario.

**Learn more:** [Microsoft-hosted agents - Azure Pipelines](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/agents/hosted)

questions.domain: Design and implement a source control strategy
questions.question:
You have an Azure key vault named KV1 and three web servers.  
  
You plan to deploy an app named App1 to the web servers.  
  
You need to ensure that App1 can retrieve a secret from KV1. The solution must meet the following requirements:  
  
• Minimize the number of permission grants required.  

• Follow the principle of least privilege.  
  
What should you include in the solution?
questions.explanation: A user-assigned managed identity can be shared across multiple resources and granted permissions once, satisfying the requirement to minimize permission grants. System-assigned identities (B) are unique per resource, requiring separate permissions for each of the three web servers. User-assigned identities follow least-privilege by allowing granular access control via a single shared identity.

questions.domain: Design and implement build and release pipelines
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You have an Azure subscription that contains an Azure pipeline named Pipeline1 and a GitHub repository named Repo1. Repo1 contains Bicep modules. Pipeline1 deploys Azure resources by using the Bicep modules.  
  
You need to ensure that all releases comply with Azure Policy before they are deployed to production.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: To Pipeline1, add a step that runs a What if deployment before the deployment step.
Configure a deployment gate for Pipeline1 that uses Azure Automation to run a What If deployment.
Create an Azure DevOps build that runs on the creation of a pull request and assesses the code for compliance.
Configure a deployment gate for Pipeline1 and include the Azure DevOps Security and compliance assessment task.

questions.explanation: Deployment gates pause pipeline execution pending the outcome of defined gates. The Azure DevOps Security and Compliance Assessment task within a deployment gate evaluates Bicep templates and resources against Azure Policy requirements before allowing production deployment. This ensures compliance is verified before resources are deployed.

questions.domain: Develop a security and compliance plan
questions.question: lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are developing a Microsoft ASP.NET application that needs to support authentication. You need to authenticate users through Azure Active Directory (Azure AD). What should you do first?

options.text: Assign an enterprise application to users and groups
Create an app registration in Azure AD
Configure the application to use a SAML endpoint
Create a new OAuth token from the application
Create a membership database in an Azure SQL database

questions.explanation:
Before an ASP.NET application can authenticate users against Azure AD, it must be registered in the Azure AD tenant via an app registration. This registration defines the application's identity (Application/client ID and tenant ID), configures redirect URIs, and sets up the permissions/scopes needed for the OpenID Connect/OAuth2 authentication flow that ASP.NET apps use with Azure AD. Without this registration, there is no application identity for Azure AD to issue tokens against, so subsequent steps such as configuring token acquisition or assigning users cannot occur. Microsoft's official tutorial for preparing a web application for Azure AD authentication begins with registering the application in the Microsoft identity platform (Azure AD) as the required first step.

**Learn more:** [Tutorial: Prepare a web application for authentication - Microsoft identity platform](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/active-directory/develop/web-app-tutorial-01-register-application) · [Quickstart - Add app authentication to a web app - Azure App Service](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/app-service/scenario-secure-app-authentication-app-service)

questions.domain: Design and implement a source control strategy
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are automating the build process for a Java-based application using Azure DevOps.  
  
You need to add code coverage testing and publish the results to the pipeline.  
  
What should you use?
questions.explanation:
Cobertura is a code coverage tool for Java applications that produces XML coverage reports (typically generated via Maven, Ant, or Gradle build plugins). Azure Pipelines' Publish Code Coverage Results task natively supports the Cobertura report format (along with JaCoCo) and uses it to generate an HTML code coverage report displayed under the Code Coverage tab of the pipeline run summary. The other options don't apply to Java: Bullseye Coverage is designed for C/C++ code, MSTest is a .NET testing framework, and Coverlet is a .NET-only cross-platform code coverage library — none of these can instrument or report coverage for Java code.

**Learn more:** [Review and configure code coverage results in Azure Pipelines](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/test/review-code-coverage-results?view=azure-devops) · [PublishCodeCoverageResults@2 - Publish code coverage results v2 task](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/tasks/reference/publish-code-coverage-results-v2?view=azure-pipelines)

questions.domain: Design and implement build and release pipelines
questions.question:
You plan to deploy a solution that will include multiple microservices.  
  
You need to recommend a deployment strategy for the microservices. The solution must meet the following requirements:  
  
• Enable testing and monitoring of changes during a gradual rollout.  

• Control the number of users that will receive new code releases.  
  
Which strategy should you recommend?
questions.explanation: Progressive exposure (canary releasing) rolls a change out to a small, controllable subset of users first, letting teams test and monitor behavior before widening the rollout, which directly satisfies both requirements. Blue/green switches all traffic at once, A/B testing compares variants for business metrics rather than gradual technical rollout, and feature toggles control functionality visibility but don't inherently manage phased user exposure across infrastructure.

questions.domain: Design and implement a source control strategy
questions.question:
You use GitHub Enterprise for source control repositories. The repositories store C# code.  
  
You need to enable CodeQL scanning for the repositories.  
  
What should you do?

options.text: Configure a required GitHub Actions workflow for all the repositories.
Push a GitHub Actions workflow to all the repositories.

questions.explanation: CodeQL scanning in GitHub Enterprise is implemented through GitHub Actions workflows that perform code analysis. To enable scanning, you must push/add the CodeQL workflow file to each repository. Dependabot handles dependency vulnerabilities, not code scanning; required workflows enforce execution but don't create the scanning capability itself.

questions.domain: Develop a security and compliance plan
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are deploying a server application that will run on a Server Core installation of Windows Server 2019.  
  
You create an Azure key vault and a secret.  
  
You need to use the key vault to secure API secrets used for integrations with third-party services.  
  
Which three actions should you perform? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.  
  
(Choose three. Each correct selection is worth one point.)

options.text: Configure RBAC for the key vault.
Modify the application to access the key vault.
Configure a Key Vault access policy.
Deploy an Azure Desired State Configuration (DSC) extension.
Deploy a virtual machine that uses a system-assigned managed identity.

questions.explanation:
To let a VM retrieve secrets from Key Vault without embedding credentials, you deploy the VM with a system-assigned managed identity, which gives the VM an automatically managed Azure AD identity. You then configure a Key Vault access policy that grants that managed identity the appropriate permissions (e.g., get/list on secrets). Finally, the application itself must be modified to call the Key Vault endpoint/SDK using the managed identity's token to fetch the secret at runtime. RBAC is an alternate access-control mechanism for Key Vault and is not required when using access policies, and deploying a DSC extension does not address secret retrieval via managed identity.

**Learn more:** [Assign a Key Vault access policy](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/key-vault/general/assign-access-policy-portal) · [How to use managed identities for Azure resources on a VM to access Key Vault](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/active-directory/managed-identities-azure-resources/tutorial-windows-vm-access-nonaad)

questions.domain: Develop a security and compliance plan
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],Your company uses the following resources:  
  
- Windows Server 2019 container images hosted in an Azure Container Registry  
- Azure virtual machines running the latest version of Ubuntu  
- An Azure Log Analytics workspace  
- Azure Active Directory (Azure AD)  
- An Azure key vault  
  
For which two of these resources can you receive vulnerability assessments in Azure Security Center? Each correct answer presents part of the solution. (Choose two.)  
  
NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

options.text: the Azure virtual machines that run the latest version of Ubuntu
The Windows Server 2019 container images hosted in the Azure Container Registry.

questions.explanation:
Azure Security Center (Microsoft Defender for Cloud) offers native vulnerability assessment for Azure virtual machines through its integrated vulnerability scanner (based on the Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management/Qualys engine), which supports both Windows and Linux VMs, including Ubuntu. It also offers vulnerability assessment for container images stored in Azure Container Registry through Microsoft Defender for container registries, which scans ACR images—including Windows Server container images—for known vulnerabilities as they are pushed or continuously in the registry. Log Analytics workspaces, Azure AD, and Key Vault do not receive this type of vulnerability (CVE) scanning from Security Center; they instead receive general security recommendations and configuration hardening guidance.

**Learn more:** [Vulnerability management for containers - Microsoft Defender for Cloud](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/defender-for-cloud/agentless-vulnerability-assessment-azure) · [Microsoft Defender for container registries - the benefits and features](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/defender-for-cloud/defender-for-container-registries-introduction)

questions.domain: Develop a security and compliance plan
questions.question:
You are creating a dashboard in Azure Boards.  
  
You need to visualize the time from when work starts on a work item until the work item is closed.  
  
Which type of widget should you use?
questions.explanation: Cycle time measures the time from when work starts on a work item until it is closed, capturing the active work duration. Lead time, by contrast, measures from when the work item is created until it is closed, including waiting time. Velocity and cumulative flow measure team productivity and workflow status respectively, not individual work item duration.

questions.domain: Implement an instrumentation strategy
questions.question:
You are developing an Azure Pipelines pipeline.  
  
You need to configure a check in the pipeline that will query Azure Boards to ensure that there are no active work item issues before the pipeline deploys a build to production.  
  
Which type of check should you implement?
questions.explanation: Pre-deployment gates allow you to configure automated checks that query systems (like Azure Boards) before deployment proceeds. This check mechanism can query for active work items and prevent deployment if issues exist. Post-deployment approvals occur after deployment, manual validations are interactive prompts, and approvals are for human decision-making rather than automated queries.

questions.domain: Design and implement a source control strategy
questions.question:
Solution: Implement a pull request strategy that uses fast-forward merges.  
  
Does this achieve the goal?
questions.explanation: A fast-forward merge preserves all commits from the source branch in the target branch and merely moves the target branch pointer forward. It therefore does not reduce the number of commits in the master branch; a squash merge is used when the pull request history must be condensed.

questions.domain: Design and implement build and release pipelines
questions.question:
Solution: You implement a pull request strategy that uses squash merges.  
  
Does this satisfy the goal?
questions.explanation:
A squash merge condenses all commits from a pull request’s source branch into one new commit on the target branch. This produces a linear target-branch history with fewer commits, reducing the history volume in the master branch.\
\
**Learn more:** [Merge strategies and squash merge - Azure Repos](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/repos/git/merging-with-squash?view=azure-devops)

questions.domain: Design and implement a source control strategy
questions.question:
Solution: You implement a pull request strategy that uses an explicit merge.  
  
Does this achieve the goal?
questions.explanation: An explicit merge preserves the individual commits from the pull request and adds a merge commit to the target branch history. This increases rather than reduces the master branch’s history volume; squash merging is the strategy that combines the pull request changes into a single commit.

questions.domain: Design and implement a source control strategy
questions.question:
Solution: Implement a pull request strategy that uses a three-way merge.  
  
Does this achieve the goal?
questions.explanation:
A three-way merge preserves the source branch’s commit history and adds a merge commit to the target branch, rather than condensing history. Reducing the history volume requires a squash merge, which combines the pull request’s changes into one commit on the target branch.\
\
**Learn more:** [Merge strategies and squash merge - Azure Repos](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/repos/git/merging-with-squash?view=azure-devops) · [Git branch policies and settings - Azure Repos](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/repos/git/branch-policies?view=azure-devops)

questions.domain: Design and implement a source control strategy
questions.question:
Solution: Implement a pull request strategy that uses a three-way merge.  
  
Does this achieve the goal?
questions.explanation:
With Docker-based applications in Azure Pipelines, one documented approach is to build and test using a multi-stage Dockerfile: the build and test steps run inside the container as separate stages, and because the test outputs stay within the intermediate build stage(s), they are never copied out or published back to the Azure DevOps pipeline. This differs from approaches that use the Publish Test Results task (or copy test result files out of the container) to explicitly surface test results in the pipeline's Tests tab. A single-stage Dockerfile lacks this stage isolation, an AKS pod is a deployment/runtime construct rather than a build-time testing mechanism, and a Docker Compose file is used to orchestrate multiple containers rather than to isolate test execution within a build.

**Learn more:** [PublishTestResults@2 - Publish Test Results v2 task | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/tasks/reference/publish-test-results-v2?view=azure-pipelines) · [Build container images to deploy apps - Azure Pipelines | Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/ecosystems/containers/build-image?view=azure-devops)

questions.domain: Design and implement a source control strategy
questions.question:
lassName":"button hollow icon-accent icon-only question-actions"}],You are developing an ASP.NET Core application.  
  
You want to create an application utilization baseline by collecting telemetry data.  
  
You need to add code to the application so that it captures the telemetry data. The solution must minimize the cost of storing the telemetry data.  
  
Which two actions should you take? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.  
  
(Choose two.)

options.text: Add the <InitialSamplingPercentage>99</InitialSamplingPercentage> parameter to the ApplicationInsights.config file.
From the code of the application, enable adaptive sampling.
From the code of the application, add Azure Application Insights telemetry.
Add the <MaxTelemetryItemsPerSecond>5</MaxTelemetryItemsPerSecond> parameter to the ApplicationInsights.config file.
From the code of the application, disable adaptive sampling.

questions.explanation:
Capturing telemetry for a usage baseline requires instrumenting the application with Azure Application Insights telemetry collection in code. To keep storage costs low while still gathering representative data, Application Insights' adaptive sampling should be enabled (it is the SDK's default behavior), as it dynamically reduces the volume of telemetry sent to the service based on traffic while maintaining accurate aggregated metrics, thereby minimizing data ingestion and storage costs. Manually setting fixed sampling percentages or item-per-second limits in the config file, or disabling adaptive sampling, does not achieve the same cost-effective, self-adjusting reduction in telemetry volume.

**Learn more:** [Sampling in Application Insights](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-monitor/app/sampling)
